title: Balaji & Benedict Evans: When Tech Breaks Industries

reader_summary.headline: Balaji and Benedict Evans explain how AI breaks industries and changes technology adoption.
reader_summary.overview: The episode argues that technology is most interesting during its transition phase, not after it becomes normal. Guests explain how AI creates new opportunities while disrupting old industries like telecom. They also discuss how humans must still verify complex code and how future systems will combine language with physical world data.

key_points.text: A technology is most interesting during its transition phase, not after everyone understands it.
key_points.evidence_quote: The moment you finally understand a technology is often the moment you should stop paying attention to it.

key_points.text: New platforms like AI create fresh opportunities because old market spaces have been filled.
key_points.evidence_quote: I would be looking around AI. Because that's a new platform. And you know, there's a lot, all the white, the old white space got filled in and now you've got a whole bunch of new white space.

key_points.text: New technology often disrupts specific parts of an industry while leaving the core business model of established companies unchanged.
key_points.evidence_quote: The iPhone demolished the existing cellular industry really having an effect on telcos. Telcos kind of hoped that they were going to do all these services, but that was never going to happen.

notes: This episode originally appeared on the Network State Podcast. Balaji Srinivasan and Benedict Evans sit down in Singapore for a wide-ranging conversation on the mechanics of disruption. Evans, a former Andreessen Horowitz partner who now writes one of tech's most-read newsletters, argues that the conversation about any technology peaks during the transition—not at 0% or 100% adoption. They cover AI's real capabilities and limits, the politics of technological disruption, why crypto's killer metric is block space, and what smart glasses, elevator attendants, and the elephant graph reveal about how change works.
